1.note: See how you translated a similar introduction in Psalms 49:1–4.

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

1.q: הַאֲזִ֣ינָ⁠ה עַ֭מִּ⁠י תּוֹרָתִ֑⁠י הַטּ֥וּ אָ֝זְנְ⁠כֶ֗ם לְ⁠אִמְרֵי־פִֽ⁠י
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how your team has decided to translate parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hear my teaching, my people; yes, listen to the words of my mouth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **teaching**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen to what I teach you]

Asaph is using this possessive form **my people** to indicate that he is addressing the Israelites as a leader or teacher among them, not to indicate that they belong to him personally. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fellow Israelites] or [people of Israel]

Asaph is speaking of paying careful attention to his teaching as if his audience could physically **incline** their **ears** toward him in order to listen better. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [pay close attention] or [listen carefully]

Here, **the words of my mouth** represents what a person says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what I say]

2.q: אֶפְתְּחָ֣ה בְ⁠מָשָׁ֣ל פִּ֑⁠י אַבִּ֥יעָה חִ֝יד֗וֹת מִנִּי־קֶֽדֶם
2.note: See the note on 78:1 or in the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on translating parallelisms. Alternate translation: [I will open my mouth in parables, yes, I will sing about hidden things from the past]

Asaph is using **I will open my mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will speak” or “I will begin to teach.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak] or [I will begin to teach]

A **parable** is a type of teaching that uses comparisons, stories, or wise sayings to communicate deeper truths. If your readers would not be familiar with this concept, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in wise sayings] or [in instructive stories]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **parables** and **riddles**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [my mouth in symbolic sayings; I will pour out what is difficult to understand from antiquity] or [my mouth by speaking metaphorically; I will pour out enigmatic sayings from antiquity]

Asaph is speaking of sharing wisdom as if he were **pouring out riddles** like liquid from a container. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will utter riddles] or [I will proclaim mysteries]

3.note: The terms **heard** and **learned** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [These are things that we know well, things]

Asaph is speaking of earlier generations of Israelites as if they were **fathers**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that our forefathers] or [that those who came before us]

4.note: Asaph is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [We will certainly tell these things to their descendants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about the praiseworthy deeds of Yahweh]

The phrase **his strength, and his wonders** expresses a single idea. The word **strength** tells more about **wonders**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [his powerful wonders] or [the mighty miracles]

5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **testimony** and **law**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what he decreed and commanded] or [his requirements and commands]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent all the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, the Israelite nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the people of Jacob and … a law among the people of Israel] or [among the descendants of Jacob and … a law among the descendants of Israel]

6.note: **So that** marks the rest of verses 6–8 as the goal or purpose of verse five. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [He commanded this in order that the generation to come]

6.q: לְמַ֤עַן יֵדְע֨וּ ׀ דּ֣וֹר אַ֭חֲרוֹן בָּנִ֣ים יִוָּלֵ֑דוּ
6.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [so that the generation to come might know his decrees, and so that the children not yet born might also know them]

The psalmist is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “take action” or “come along.” He does not mean that the children will literally stand up. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they in their turn will tell] or [and they will then tell]

7.note: The psalmist is speaking of **confidence** as if it were something that could be physically **placed** in a secure location. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they would trust in God] or [And they would rely on God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they would hope in God] or [And they would confidently trust in God]

8.note: The terms **stubborn** and **rebellious** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very obstinate generation] or [an extremely defiant generation]

Here, **heart** represents the inner disposition and loyalty of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were not inwardly loyal] or [whose inner disposition was not right]

Here, **spirit** represents the inner person or will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were not committed and faithful to God]

9.note: The psalmist is using **turned back on the day of battle** as a common expression of the culture to mean “retreated in battle” or “fled when they should have fought.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fled when they should have fought] or [retreated instead of fighting]

The psalmist is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when it was time to fight] or [at the time of battle]

10.q: לֹ֣א שָׁ֭מְרוּ בְּרִ֣ית אֱלֹהִ֑ים וּ֝⁠בְ⁠תוֹרָת֗⁠וֹ מֵאֲנ֥וּ לָ⁠לֶֽכֶת
10.note: See the note on 78:1 or the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on how to translate parallelisms. Alternate translation: [They did not keep the covenant with God; indeed, they refused to obey his law]

The psalmist is using this possessive form, **the covenant of God**, to mean the covenant that God had made with the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the covenant that God had made with them] or [God’s covenant]

The psalmist is speaking of obeying God’s law as if it were a path one could **walk** on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they refused to obey his law]

11.note: The psalmist is not distinguishing the **wonders that he had shown them** from other wonderful things that God had not shown them. The psalmist is reminding the people about the character of God’s deeds that they forgot. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [which were wonderful things that he had shown them]

12.note: The word **Zoan** is the name of a city.

Here, **their fathers** represents their ancestors who were present to see the marvelous things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when their ancestors were present] or [while their ancestors were watching]

13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a heap** is a vertical structure, so **the waters** stood upright. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he made the waters stand upright like a solid wall]

14.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all the night he led them with the light of fire]

By **the cloud** and **the light of fire**, the psalmist means the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21–22). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the pillar of cloud … with the pillar of fire]

15.note: The pronoun **He** refers to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God split open]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the deep** has limitless water, so God provided limitless water for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he gave them water as limitless as the deep]

The psalmist says **and he gave drink abundantly as the deep** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he gave them an enormous amount of water to drink]

16.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **rivers** are abundant and continuous in their flow, so was the water that God brought from the rock. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in great abundance] or [in a continuous stream]

17.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites, the ancestors of those whom the psalmist is addressing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelite people added] or [And those ancestors added]

The psalmist uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast between God’s gracious provision and the people’s sinful response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But they added still to sin against him] or [Yet they added still to sin against him]

18.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **by asking for food for their appetite** to state the reason for the result that **they tested God in their hearts**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [And they tested God in their hearts when they asked for food for their appetite]

Here, **hearts** represents the inner thoughts and attitudes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their minds] or [inwardly]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **appetite**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what they craved] or [for what they desired to eat]

19.note: The Israelites are using the question form to express doubt about God’s ability to provide for them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God cannot arrange a table in the wilderness!] or [Surely God is not able to arrange a table in the wilderness!]

The Israelites are speaking of God providing food as if he were **arranging a table** for a meal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [provide food for us]

20.q: הֲ⁠גַם־לֶ֭חֶם י֣וּכַל תֵּ֑ת אִם־יָכִ֖ין שְׁאֵ֣ר לְ⁠עַמּֽ⁠וֹ
20.note: The Israelites are using the question form to express their doubt that God can provide different kinds of food. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [But surely he cannot give bread also! Surely he cannot provide meat for his people!] or [But he is not able to give bread also. He cannot provide meat for his people.]

The people are speaking of themselves in the third person as **his people** to acknowledge their relationship with God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for us, his people]

21.note: The expression **a fire was kindled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh kindled a fire against Jacob] or [and Yahweh’s anger burned against Jacob]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s anger as if it were **a fire** that could be **kindled**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh became furiously angry against Jacob] or [and Yahweh’s anger burned against Jacob]

Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and also his anger burned against Israel] or [and also he became angry with Israel]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent the entire nation descended from this patriarch. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [against the people of Jacob … against the people of Israel] or [against the nation of Israel]

22.q: כִּ֤י לֹ֣א הֶ֭אֱמִינוּ בֵּ⁠אלֹהִ֑ים וְ⁠לֹ֥א בָ֝טְח֗וּ בִּֽ⁠ישׁוּעָתֽ⁠וֹ
22.note: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since they did not believe in God and did not trust in his salvation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and that he would save them]

23.note: The psalmist uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between the Israelites’ unbelief and God’s gracious provision. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But he commanded] or [Even so, he commanded]

23.q: וַ⁠יְצַ֣ו שְׁחָקִ֣ים מִ⁠מָּ֑עַל וְ⁠דַלְתֵ֖י שָׁמַ֣יִם פָּתָֽח
23.note: The psalmist is speaking of the sky as if it were a building with **doors** that God opened. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yet he gave orders to the sky above and caused the heavens to open]

The psalmist is speaking of **the clouds** as if they were living things that could hear and obey God’s commands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He controlled the clouds]

24.note: The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a weather phenomenon, and **he rained down manna** from the sky. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He caused manna to fall down from the sky]
The phrase **the grain of heaven** could mean: (1) the grain that angels eat or (2) the grain that came from heaven. The next verse supports the first meaning.

The psalmist is using **grain** to represent all of the manna that God provided. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and … the food from heaven] or [and … the provision from heaven]

25.note: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **Man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People ate]

The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the food] or [the grain]
The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the mighty** refers to angels. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [of angels]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **satisfaction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [enough food to satisfy them] or [abundant food]

27.note: The psalmist is speaking of the meat as if it were rain that God **rained down** on the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He caused meat to fall on them in great abundance] or [He gave them a huge amount of meat]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he rained down birds of wing as numerous as the sands of the sea]
It might seem that the expression **birds of wing** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [birds]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **birds** that are characterized by having **wings**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [winged birds] or [flying birds]

The psalmist says **like dust** and **as the sands of the sea** as extreme statements for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [in great quantities and … beyond counting]

28.note: The pronoun **his** refers to the people of Israel, not to God. The psalmist is describing the birds falling into the Israelites’ camp and near their tents. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [They fell in the middle of the Israelites’ camp, all around the Israelites’ tents]
Here, **his** refers to the Israelites. See the book introduction for more information.

29.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **craving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He gave them what they craved]

30.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 78:29.

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 78:21.

The psalmist is speaking of the young men dying as if God were physically forcing them to **bow down** to the ground. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he struck down the young men of Israel] or [and he made the young men of Israel fall dead]

32.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the wonderful things he did] or [that he could do wonderful things]

33.note: This is poetic language. The psalmist moves from shorter units of time (**days**) to longer units (**years**) to emphasize the completeness of God’s judgment. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [So he ended their lives quickly, like a breath, and their years were full of fear]

The psalmist is referring to God ending the lives of the Israelites in a polite way by using the phrase **he consumed their days**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [So he ended their days] or [So he caused their days to vanish]

The psalmist is speaking of **their days** as if they were something that could be **consumed** (used up) **in a vapor** (as quickly as a puff of breath disappears). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So he caused their days to quickly vanish like vapor] or [So he caused their days to pass swiftly like a breath]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he consumed their years in terror]

Here, **their days** and **their years** represent their lives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lives … and their lives]

34.note: The psalmist is describing repeated events, not a single occurrence. The word **When** indicates that this pattern happened multiple times. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a word or phrase that shows this repetition. Alternate translation: [Each time God afflicted them, they would seek him]

35.q: וַֽ֭⁠יִּזְכְּרוּ כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֣ים צוּרָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠אֵ֥ל עֶ֝לְיוֹן גֹּאֲלָֽ⁠ם
35.note: See the note on 78:1 or the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on how to translate parallelisms. Alternate translation: [They would remember that God Most High was their rock and redeemer]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a **rock** that provided protection and stability. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture, or you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God was their refuge] or [God was their protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they would remember that God Most High was their rescuer]

36.note: Here, **with their mouth** and **with their tongues** represent what the people said by using their mouth and words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by what they said to him and … in what they told him]

37.note: Here, **hearts** represents the people’s inner desires and commitment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they were not truly committed to him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **steadfast**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they were not loyal to him in their hearts] or [And they did not remain faithful toward him in their hearts]

38.note: The psalmist is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with an expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [Many times he chose to be patient with his people]

Here, **nose** represents anger. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he held back his anger] or [he restrained his anger]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s anger as if it were something physical that God **held back** to keep it from going out toward the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he restrained his anger] or [he controlled his anger]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s wrath as if it were something dormant that he could **stir up** or arouse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and did not cause his full wrath to awaken] or [and did not unleash the full extent of his anger]

39.note: Here, **flesh** represents the weakness and frailty of human nature. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they were weak and frail] or [they were mortal]

The psalmist is speaking of human beings as if they were **a wind going and it does not return**. He means that human life is brief and fragile, like a wind that blows by once and then is gone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [mortal beings whose lives quickly end]

41.note: The psalmist is using the expression **they returned and they tested** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they repeatedly tested.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They tested God again and again] or [They continually tested God]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to describe the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and grieved the holy God with whom the Israelites are in a covenant relationship]
The expression **the Holy One of Israel** is a title for God.

42.note: Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his power] or [his strength]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **day**. He means the time in general when God redeemed the Israelites from Egypt. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the time]

Here, **the adversary** represents Egypt and Pharaoh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he redeemed them from Egypt] or [he redeemed them from Pharaoh]

43.note: See how you translated this in 78:12. **Zoan** was a city in Egypt.

45.note: Here, **the frog** represents frogs in general, not one particular frog. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the frogs]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he sent the frog]

46.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **labor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what they had labored to produce]

Here, **labor** represents the produce or results of their labor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and what their labor produced] or [and the fruit of their labor]

48.note: The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a commander who **gave over** the Egyptians’ **cattle to the hail** as if the hail were an enemy army that would attack them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he caused the hail to kill their cattle and gave their livestock] or [And he allowed the hail to strike down their cattle and gave their livestock]

49.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **the burning of his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among them his fierce anger] or [among them his burning anger]

The terms **fury**, **indignation**, and **distress** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great wrath]

49.q: יְשַׁלַּח־בָּ֨⁠ם ׀ חֲר֬וֹן אַפּ֗⁠וֹ עֶבְרָ֣ה וָ⁠זַ֣עַם וְ⁠צָרָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁלַ֗חַת מַלְאֲכֵ֥י רָעִֽים
49.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **fury**, **indignation**, **distress**, and **calamity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [He furiously and indignantly distressed them with disastrous messengers]

49.q: יְשַׁלַּח־בָּ֨⁠ם ׀ חֲר֬וֹן אַפּ֗⁠וֹ עֶבְרָ֣ה וָ⁠זַ֣עַם וְ⁠צָרָ֑ה מִ֝שְׁלַ֗חַת מַלְאֲכֵ֥י רָעִֽים
49.note: The psalmist is speaking of **fury and indignation and distress** as if they were living things that could be sent as **messengers** to carry out God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He vented on them his great anger and fury, causing them trouble and disaster]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s anger as if it were a weapon or force that **He sent** out to strike the Egyptians. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His fierce anger struck them with fury and indignation] or [He attacked them with his fierce anger]

50.note: The psalmist is speaking of **his anger** as if it were something that could travel along a **path**. He means that God fully released his anger against the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He gave full vent to his anger] or [He released his anger without restraint]

The psalmist is speaking of the lives of the Egyptians as if they were something God could physically give **over to the plague**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but allowed them to die from the plague] or [but caused the plague to kill them]

51.note: The psalmist is using **the beginning of strength** as a common expression of the culture to mean the **firstborn** sons. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the firstborn sons] or [the oldest sons]

Here, **tents** represents the families who lived in them, and **Ham** represents the people of Egypt, who were descended from him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the households of Egypt] or [among the people of Egypt]

52.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** need a shepherd to guide and care for them, so did God’s people need God to guide and care for them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he made his people journey, guiding and caring for them like a shepherd does for sheep, and he led them, protecting them like a shepherd protects a flock in the wilderness]

53.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **security**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [securely] or [safely]

54.note: The pronoun **he** refers to God, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And God brought the Israelites]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **the border** that is characterized by **his holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the border of the land he had set apart] or [the border of his holy land]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [of what is holy to him] or [of what he had set apart]

Here, **his right hand** represents the power of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he acquired by his power] or [that his power acquired]

55.note: The pronoun **he** refers to God, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God drove out nations from before the Israelites]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the Canaanites whom God **caused them to fall in a portion of inheritance**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you could use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and caused them to be defeated in each portion that Israel inherited] or [and defeated them in each portion that Israel inherited as they came to it]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean a portion for inheriting. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [in each portion inherited by Israel] or [in each portion that Israel inherited]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and gave each tribe a portion to inherit] or [and gave each tribe of Israel a portion as their own]

56.note: The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between God’s provision and the people’s rebellion. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Despite all this, they tested and rebelled] or [Even so, they tested and rebelled]

The terms **tested** and **rebelled** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [But they continually pushed back] or [But they stubbornly rebelled]

57.q: וַ⁠יִּסֹּ֣גוּ וַֽ֭⁠יִּבְגְּדוּ כַּ⁠אֲבוֹתָ֑⁠ם נֶ֝הְפְּכ֗וּ כְּ⁠קֶ֣שֶׁת רְמִיָּֽה
57.note: For more information on translating parallelism, see the note at 78:1. Alternate translation: [They turned back and acted treacherously like their fathers, being as unreliable as a bow of deceit]

The point of this comparison is that just as **their fathers** were unfaithful to God, so were the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [in the same unfaithful way as their fathers]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bow of deceit** is unreliable and does not shoot straight, so were the Israelites unreliable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as unreliable as a faulty bow]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a bow** that is characterized by **deceit**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into a deceitful bow] or [as a faulty bow]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into a deceitful bow] or [as a faulty bow]

58.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **jealousy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [they caused him to be jealous]

59.note: The term translated as **and** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [God heard, and as a result, he was furious] or [When God heard, he was furious]

60.note: The term translated as **And** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore, he abandoned the dwelling of Shiloh] or [So he abandoned the dwelling of Shiloh]

61.note: Here, **his strength** represents the box of the covenant, which showed God’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And he allowed the box to be captured] or [And he let the box that showed his power be captured]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what showed he was strong] or [the box that showed his power]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **captivity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be captured] or [to those who would capture it]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he gave his splendor]

Here, **his splendor** represents the box of the covenant, and **the hand of the enemy** represents their power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use equivalent expressions or plain language. Alternate translation: [and his glorious box into the power of the enemy] or [and the box that showed his splendor to be controlled by the enemy]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **splendor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what was splendid to him] or [and the ark that showed he was glorious]

62.note: Here, **the sword** represents warfare or violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he allowed his people to be killed in battle] or [And he delivered his people over to violent death]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. See how you translated this in 78:55. Alternate translation: [and … with the people he had chosen]

63.note: The phrases **Fire consumed his young men** and **his virgins were not praised** mean opposite things but work together to show the devastating completeness of the judgment. For emphasis, the psalmist is describing both the death of young men and the corresponding lack of marriage celebrations. If a speaker of your language would not use this kind of contrast, in your translation you can convey the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [Fire consumed his young men so that his virgins had no weddings]

The psalmist speaks of **Fire** as if it were a person that could actively consume people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His young men died in fires] or [His young men were burned to death]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and no one praised his virgins in wedding songs] or [and no one sang wedding songs for his virgins]

64.note: Here, **the sword** represents violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [died in battle] or [were killed in war]

65.note: The psalmist uses the word **Then** to indicate a contrast between God’s judgment and his intervention. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But then the Lord awoke] or [After this, the Lord awoke]

The psalmist speaks of **the Lord** as if he were a person who could sleep and wake up. He means that God had seemed inactive during the time of judgment but then became active again to help his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then the Lord acted as if he had awakened from sleep] or [Then the Lord began to act again after seeming to be inactive]

The point of this comparison is that just as **one sleeping** must wake up before acting, so the Lord resumed acting after a period of seeming inactivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like someone who had been asleep]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a mighty man** who has been drinking wine might shout loudly and powerfully, so the Lord acted with great power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a powerful warrior shouting with great strength]

66.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **perpetuity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a shame that lasts forever] or [permanent disgrace]

68.note: The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between rejecting Joseph and Ephraim and choosing Judah. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Instead, he chose the tribe of Judah]

Here, **Mount Zion** represents the tribe of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Judah’s descendants, who]

69.q: וַ⁠יִּ֣בֶן כְּמוֹ־רָ֭מִים מִקְדָּשׁ֑⁠וֹ כְּ֝⁠אֶ֗רֶץ יְסָדָ֥⁠הּ לְ⁠עוֹלָֽם
69.note: The phrase **he built his sanctuary like the heights** is parallel to the statement **like the earth he founded it forever** and clarifies the relationship between the sanctuary’s grandeur and its permanence. Alternate translation: [And he built his sanctuary to be as exalted as the heavens and as permanent as the earth]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the heights** are exalted and majestic, so is God’s sanctuary. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as exalted as the heavens]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the earth** is permanent and enduring, so God **founded** his sanctuary to last **forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as enduring as the earth, he founded it to last forever]

71.note: The term translated as **to** indicates that what follows is a purpose or goal of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to shepherd Jacob his people] or [so that he would shepherd Jacob his people]

The psalmist is speaking of **Jacob his people** as if they were sheep that needed someone **to shepherd** them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to lead and care for Jacob his people] or [to rule over Jacob his people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people who belonged to him] or [the people he had chosen as his own]

72.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **integrity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with an honest heart] or [with a pure heart]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **his heart** that is characterized by **integrity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to his honest heart]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **skillfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with his skillful hands he guided them] or [and he guided them skillfully]

Here, **his hands** represents the actions and capabilities of David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with his skill he guided them] or [and he guided them with his abilities]
